subject: Your raise lost to inflation. The Bank may hike anyway.
bodyMarkdown:
Wages grew 2.0% last month. Prices grew 3.0%. That gap is the whole story of this economy right now, and the Bank of Canada has just said it might raise rates into it.

## The August numbers, plainly

Employment fell by 42,000 in August, Statistics Canada reported on Friday. Economists had penciled in a gain of about 15,000, so the miss was not small. The unemployment rate did not move, holding at 6.4%, which sounds like stability until you look at why. The **employment rate**, the share of working-age people who actually hold a job, slipped to 60.8%. People left the workforce instead of showing up in the unemployment count.

The sector detail says where the damage landed. Business, building and other support services lost 20,000 positions. Public administration shed 8,800, natural resources 7,700, utilities 5,600. Manufacturing went the other way and added 22,000.

Worth keeping in view: April through July added 181,000 jobs between them. One soft month after four strong ones is not a collapse. It is the first month the direction changed.

## The wage number is the one to watch

Average hourly wages rose 2.0% year over year in August, up 71 cents to $37.02. In July the figure was 2.8%. Leaving out the distorted pandemic year of 2021, that is the slowest wage growth since November 2017.

Now set it against inflation running at 3.0%. If your pay moved in line with the average, you lost roughly a percentage point of buying power over the year. That gap already showed up in your paycheque.

Here is the part I find strange. Weak wage growth normally hands a central bank room to cut. Instead, on September 2, when the Bank held its policy rate at 2.25% for a seventh consecutive decision, Governor Tiff Macklem said policymakers were prepared to raise borrowing costs more than once if inflation stayed too high.

## Why the Bank is threatening hikes into a soft job market

Because this inflation is not coming from wages. Macklem pointed at oil prices pushed up by the conflict with Iran, and at tariffs. Neither one answers to a policy rate. You can make a mortgage in Richmond Hill more expensive and it will not change what a barrel of crude costs.

On Monday that second pressure gets heavier. Canada's counter-tariffs take effect at 12:01 a.m. on September 8, covering more than 700 American products worth $27.6 billion at rates of 15%, 25% and 50%, matching Washington's rates dollar for dollar. Steel, aluminum, furniture, clothing and apparel sit in the 50% band. Appliances, dairy and seafood are at 25%.

Tariffs show up as higher prices at the till. So the Bank is looking at inflation it cannot fix with rates, sitting on top of a job market that higher rates would make worse.

## The takeaway

Watch the September inflation reading when it lands in October, and watch whether the increase stays inside tariffed goods and fuel or starts spreading into services and rents. If it stays put, the hiking talk is a signal meant to keep expectations anchored rather than a plan, and 2.25% survives the October 28 decision. If it spreads, the threat is real and mortgage renewals get worse before they get better. Either way, if you are negotiating a raise this fall, 2.0% is the number your employer will quote you and 3.0% is the number you actually need.
